policy: none supplied; policy-based checks report REVIEW unless they meet the recommendation

findings.rationale: Root is a known account name with full control of the host. Blocking direct root login forces attackers to guess a username as well, and leaves a record of which named user became root.
findings.remediation: Set 'PermitRootLogin no'. First confirm that a non-root account can log in and use sudo.

findings.expected: no, or a controlled exception approved by policy
findings.rationale: Passwords can be guessed or reused, while key-based login cannot be brute-forced in the same way. Some organisations still allow passwords with compensating controls, so 'yes' is a policy decision.
findings.remediation: Set 'PasswordAuthentication no' once every user has a working key, or record an approved exception in the policy file.

findings.rationale: If allowed, an account with an empty password can be logged into by anyone who can reach the SSH port. The starter file lists this check's severity as 'pass'; that is a result, so this baseline rates the risk as high.

findings.expected: no, unless policy records that it is required
findings.rationale: The manual warns that X11 forwarding may add exposure to the server and to client displays. Some users need graphical programs over SSH, so 'yes' is a policy decision.
findings.remediation: Set 'X11Forwarding no' if nobody needs it. Ubuntu's shipped sshd_config sets it to yes, so check the file as well as the upstream default.

references.title: sshd_config(5), Ubuntu 24.04 manual page
references.detail: X11Forwarding: default is no; describes the additional exposure; Debian-based packages ship it set to yes

findings.expected: 4 or lower, or a value approved by policy
findings.rationale: This limits authentication attempts per connection, which slows password guessing. A higher value is allowed only if policy approves it.
findings.remediation: Set 'MaxAuthTries 4', or record the approved value in the policy file.

references.title: CIS Benchmark for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS v1.0.0, as mapped by ComplianceAsCode (CIS PDF not read directly)
references.detail: Control 5.1.16: Ensure sshd MaxAuthTries is configured (mapped value 4)

findings.expected: the idle timeout approved by policy, in seconds
findings.rationale: A value of 0 means the server sends no client-alive messages, so it does not detect unresponsive clients. The right timeout depends on the organisation, so the checker needs an approved value to compare against.
findings.remediation: Set an approved value such as 'ClientAliveInterval 300' with 'ClientAliveCountMax 2', and record it in the policy file.

references.title: CIS Benchmark for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS v1.0.0, as mapped by ComplianceAsCode (CIS PDF not read directly)
references.detail: Control 5.1.7: Ensure sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured (mapping notes CIS requires values above 0)

references.title: sshd_config(5), Ubuntu 24.04 manual page
references.detail: ClientAliveInterval: default is 0, meaning messages are not sent

findings.expected: an explicit list of accounts approved by policy
findings.rationale: By default every user may log in over SSH, including accounts that never need it. Only the organisation knows which accounts are approved, so the checker needs a policy list to compare against.
findings.remediation: Set 'AllowUsers' to the approved accounts, and confirm your own account is listed before restarting SSH so you are not locked out.
